This vignette gives the exact definitions behind `propensity_sensitivity()`. Every diagnostic
uses the covariates and the treatment only; none uses the outcome.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| n | number of patients |
| T_i | treatment, 1 = treated, 0 = untreated |
| m | one propensity model: one algorithm with one setting or seed |
| e_m(i) | cross-fitted probability of treatment from model m, clipped to [0.001, 0.999] |
| l_m(i) | logit of e_m(i) |
| r_m(i) | percentile rank of l_m(i) among all n patients (rank divided by n) |
| c_m(i) | the untreated partner matched to treated patient i under model m |

## The model set and the quality gate

The default set of `propensity_sensitivity()` and of `fit_propensity_models()`, the set evaluated in a manuscript in preparation, has logistic
regression (main effects), Bayesian additive regression trees (`dbarts::bart2`, probit link,
default priors, 75 trees, four chains of 500 burn-in and 500 kept draws, posterior mean
probability) and a generalized random forest (`grf::probability_forest`, 2,000 honest trees), the
two tree algorithms with three seeds each: seven models.

A faster set is available with `algorithms = c("logistic_regression", "random_forest",
"gradient_boosting")`: a random forest (500 trees, `mtry = floor(sqrt(p))`, node size 10) and
gradient boosting (depth 3, shrinkage 0.05, bagging fraction 0.8; the number of trees chosen once
by 5-fold cross-validation and then frozen). It is not part of that evaluation.

Every score is **cross-fitted**: the patients are split into five folds shared by all models, and
each patient's score comes from a model fitted on the other four folds. In-sample tree scores are
overfit; cross-fitting keeps every model honest. (`cross_fit = FALSE` gives the in-sample scores
that `MatchIt` would use.)

A model counts as "equally reasonable" only if

```
cross-fitted log-loss  <=  1.05 x (best model's log-loss)
max |SMD| on main terms after matching  <=  (best model's max |SMD| on main terms) + 0.10
max |SMD| on main terms after matching  <=  0.25
```

This is the default relative balance rule (`balance_rule = "relative"`): a model is excluded
only when its balance is clearly worse than the best model's. With a few hundred matched pairs
the largest chance SMD over several covariates often exceeds 0.10, so a fixed 0.10 limit would
exclude good models. The fixed limit is available as `balance_rule = "absolute"`
(`balance_threshold = 0.10`). If fewer than two models pass, all models are used and the result
says so. The role of the balance part of the gate is evaluated in a manuscript in preparation.

## Matching

Every model is used for 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching for the average treatment effect in the
treated (ATT), on the logit, by calling `MatchIt::matchit()` with the logit as a numeric
distance. The order is MatchIt's default for the ATT (treated patients with the largest score
first). Both matching with and without replacement are supported (the formula interface
defaults to without replacement, the common applied choice;
it is in general not consistent for the ATT, whereas matching with replacement is). The
diagnostic with and without replacement is evaluated in a manuscript in preparation.

## Rank disagreement (primary)

```
d(i) = standard deviation over models m of r_m(i)
```

Percentile ranks are used rather than logits because algorithms are calibrated differently: a
random forest and a logistic regression can order the patients the same way while their logits
differ a lot. Ranks do not change under any increasing transformation of a score, so only the
ordering of the patients counts.

```{r invariance}
logit <- c(-2, -1, 0.5, 3)
rank(logit) / 4
rank(exp(logit)) / 4    # an increasing transformation: same ranks
```

To separate model dependence from seed noise:

```
d_between(i) = SD over algorithms a of  (mean over seeds k of r_{a,k}(i))
d_within(i)  = sqrt( mean over algorithms with at least two seeds of
                     (variance over seeds k of r_{a,k}(i)) )
```

Logistic regression has a single model and no seed variance, so it is left out of `d_within`.
The study-level numbers are the mean of d(i) over treated patients and the median over treated
patients of `d_between / d_within`. **A ratio near 1 means the algorithms disagree with each
other no more than one algorithm disagrees with itself across seeds: noise, not model
dependence.** Standard deviations use the n − 1 denominator.

The logit-scale version `d_logit(i) = SD over m of l_m(i)` is reported as a secondary measure.

## Control spread (primary at the patient level)

Different partner *identities* are harmless if the untreated partners have the same covariates.
Control spread measures whether the models pick different *kinds* of untreated partners:

```
C(i)        = the distinct untreated partners matched to treated patient i across the models
s(i)        = mean pairwise Mahalanobis distance between the covariate vectors in C(i),
              with the covariance matrix of all n patients
s_scaled(i) = s(i) / (mean over treated patients of the Mahalanobis distance between a
                      treated patient and its logistic-regression match)
```

`s(i) = 0` when every model picks the same untreated partner. `s_scaled = 1` reads "the
candidate partners differ from each other as much as a typical match differs from its treated patient". Factor
covariates are expanded to dummies; constant and linearly dependent columns are dropped.

## Balance spread (study level)

After matching on each model, four balance statistics are computed with `cobalt`: the maximum
absolute standardized mean difference on main terms, the same with squares and all two-way
interactions, the energy distance, and the maximum Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. Standardized
differences use the standard deviation of the treated group, and binary covariates are
standardized too, so all covariates are on one scale. The spread is the range and the standard
deviation of each statistic across the models in use, with the worst model named.

## Pair recurrence and pair instability

```
pair recurrence, across models:     share of the models in use whose untreated partner equals
                                    i's most common untreated partner
pair instability (study level):     1 - mean over treated of the pair recurrence across models
pair recurrence, across bootstrap:  share of bootstrap refits of the logistic model that choose
                                    i's most common untreated partner, counting only refits
                                    that contain both i and that partner
```

**Pair instability** is the second summary of the same gated model set. Rank disagreement, the
primary summary, measures how differently the models order the treated patients; pair
instability counts how often they choose different untreated partners for them. The two answer
the same question from two sides, and a change of rank need not change the partner: where
untreated patients are sparse a patient's rank can move a lot while its nearest untreated patient
stays the same, and where untreated patients are dense a small move changes it. Rank disagreement is the primary summary and pair
instability is exploratory; both are evaluated in a manuscript in preparation. Report rank
disagreement first and pair instability next to it. The summary table keeps `pair_recurrence_models_mean_treated` for
backward compatibility; `pair_instability_models_mean_treated` is 1 minus it.

Pair recurrence across models lies between 1 / (number of models) and 1, so pair instability
lies between 0 and 1 - 1 / (number of models). When untreated patients are dense the recurrence
is often
near its floor; read pair instability against comparable studies, not against a cut-off.
Without the denominator correction the bootstrap version could never exceed about 0.63, because
any patient is missing from about 37 % of bootstrap samples.

## What the simulation compares against: the truth

In simulated data the expected outcome without treatment, mu0(x), is known. For each model:

```
B_m  = mean over treated i of  mu0(X_i) - mu0(X_{c_m(i)})     (imbalance-driven bias)
D    = standard deviation of B_m across the models in use     (study-level model dependence)
t(i) = standard deviation across models of mu0(X_{c_m(i)})    (patient-level model dependence)
```

**Why B contains no treatment effect.** Under the ATT with every treated patient matched, the
treated group is the same under every model; only the untreated partners change, and the
outcomes of untreated patients contain no treatment effect. So a heterogeneous treatment effect does not move the differences
between models. The simulation checks this identity numerically on every dataset of Scenario 2
(differences below 1e-10). The share of treated patients kept is reported separately, because a
caliper that drops treated patients changes the target population.

## Traps this design avoids

| Trap | What the package does |
|---|---|
| In-sample tree scores are overfit and shrink overlap | all scores are cross-fitted |
| Random-forest out-of-bag probabilities can be exactly 0 or 1 | probabilities are clipped to [0.001, 0.999] before the logit |
| Boosting re-tuned on every fit is not a fixed model | the tree count is chosen once and frozen |
| Logit-scale disagreement is large even when every model orders patients alike | percentile ranks are primary |
| Seed noise looks like model dependence | the between/within decomposition |
| Different partner identities need not mean different kinds of untreated partners | control spread uses covariate distances |
| Pair recurrence is often near its floor when untreated patients are dense | pair instability is reported as a second, exploratory summary next to rank disagreement, never alone |
| The bootstrap is not valid for the variance of matching estimators | the bootstrap is used for design stability only, never for a confidence interval |
| No outcome-free check can tell harmful from harmless misspecification | stated as a limitation; the simulation shows both cases |
